'''Erich Klinghammer''' (February 28, 1930 – October 6, 2011) was a German and American [[wolf]] [[biologist]] best known for his contributions to the fields of [[ethology]] and [[behavioural ecology]], particularly that of [[Canidae|canids]]. He was the founder of [[Wolf Park]] in [[Indiana]] and a professor of [[Ethology|animal behaviour]] at [[Purdue University]].<ref name=obit>{{cite news|volume=114|number=3|url=http://mag.uchicago.edu/university-news/university-obituaries|author=University of Chicago Magazine Staff|year=2012|title=University Obituaries|periodical=University of Chicago Magazine}}</ref>

==Education==
Erich Klinghammer was born in [[Kassel, Germany]], where he received high school education. During this time in Germany, Erich was a member of the [[Hitler Youth]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Into The Light: Erich Klinghammer|url=https://www.blackfive.net/main/2011/10/into-the-light-erich-klinghammer.html|access-date=June 20, 2021|website=BlackFive}}</ref> He emigrated to [[United States]] in 1951 and served in the [[United States Army]] from 1953 to 1955, earning [[Citizenship in the United States|United States citizenship]] through military service, and returned to higher education at the [[University of Chicago]] with support from the [[G. I. Bill]]. He graduated with a Bachelor of Arts in 1958<ref name=obit/> and continued graduate education under animal behaviorist [[Eckhard Hess]], studying [[imprinting (psychology)|imprinting]] in [[bird]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.muskingum.edu/~psych/psycweb/history/hess.htm|title=Psychology History|author=Jason Waite|year=1999|accessdate=August 31, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130929134315/http://muskingum.edu/~psych/psycweb/history/hess.htm|archive-date=September 29, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref> After discovering he was allergic to birds, he switched the focal species of his research on animal behaviour to [[Wolf|grey wolves]] donated by the [[Brookfield Zoo]] and housed in an enclosure on his property near [[Battle Ground, Indiana]]. He received his PhD in 1962 but would continue study on the captive wolves, expanding as more animals arrived.<ref name=obit/><ref name=wphist>{{cite web|url=http://wolfpark.org/about/park-history/|title=Park History|author=Wolf Park|accessdate=August 31, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130815022844/http://wolfpark.org/about/park-history/|archive-date=August 15, 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Wolf research==
Erich Klinghammer was appointed assistant professor at the University of Chicago in 1965, lecturing on ethology and [[Comparative psychology|animal psychology]]. In 1968, he transferred to the Department of Psychological Sciences at [[Purdue University]] to hold the position of associate professor, continuing his pioneering study on wolf pack dynamics and social behaviour, including early analyses of wolf howls<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Klinghammer|first1=E.|last2=Laidlaw|first2=L.|title=Analysis of 23 months of daily howl records in a captive grey wolf pack (''Canis lupus'')|journal=The Behavior and Ecology of Wolves|year=1979|pages=153–181}}</ref> and developing the techniques of socialization for wildlife in captivity.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Klinghammer|first1=E.|last2=Goodmann|first2=P.A.|title=The management and socialization of captive wolves (''Canis lupus'') at Wolf Park|year=1987|journal=Ethology Series|url=http://agris.fao.org/agris-search/search/display.do?f=2012/OV/OV201201853001853.xml;US19920025729}}</ref> His property developed into a wolf research and education facility eventually named [[Wolf Park]], officially founded in 1972 with him as director. The resident study animal population would expand to include other species of canids such as [[coyote]]s and [[red fox]]es.<ref name=wphist/>

At the time, very little was known about wolves as their behaviour was difficult to observe for prolonged periods in the wild. Extended scientific observations of wolves in captivity allowed their complex social behaviours to be characterized, information which would later be corroborated or differences examined by more extensive and advanced field studies.<ref>Klinghammer, E. (ed.) 1979. ''The Behavior and Ecology of Wolves''. New York: Garland.</ref><ref>{{cite book|author1=Mech, L. David|author2=Boitani, Luigi|title=Wolves: Behavior, Ecology, and Conservation|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_mXHuSSbiGgC|year=2003|publisher=University of Chicago Press|isbn=978-0-226-51696-7}}</ref> Together with other scientific staff at the park, Klinghammer published and maintained the Wolf Ethogram, an encyclopedia of all wolf behaviours and vocalizations recorded.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Goodmann|first1=P.A.|last2=Klinghammer|first2=E.|year=2002|title=Wolf Ethogram|series=Ethology Series}}</ref>

In his theoretical views, Klinghammer followed the approach of [[Jakob von Uexküll]] and used his concept of [[umwelt]].<ref>Pat Goodmann. ''The Wolf Park News'', 2012, p. 1–2.</ref>

In 1993, after teaching for 26 years, Erich Klinghammer retired from his position at Purdue as [[professor emeritus]]. He would continue his mission of wolf research and education at Wolf Park until passing on in 2011 at the age of 81.<ref name=obit/>

==Legacy==
Through his activities at Wolf Park, Erich Klinghammer taught and inspired many budding biologists and conservationists who would later go on to conduct significant research and conservation work on wolves and other species, including Douglas Smith, leader of the [[Yellowstone National Park]] [[Wolf reintroduction in Yellowstone#In Idaho .2F Yellowstone National Park|Wolf Project]] and Roger Pallmer, founder of the [[UK Wolf Conservation Trust]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Smith|first=Douglas|title=Decade of the Wolf: Returning the Wild to Yellowstone|year=2006|publisher=Lyons Press|isbn=1592288863|pages=256|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3m1B8XEoiyUC&dq=purdue+university+erich+klinghammer&pg=PA11}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis|url=http://trace.tennessee.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1652&context=utk_graddiss|author=Davis, Karen M.|year=2009|title=Sociality, Cognition and Social Learning in Turtles (Emydidae)|publisher=University of Tennessee}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://ukwct.org.uk/index.php?page=history|title=History - UK Wolf Conservation Trust|accessdate=June 9, 2022|author=UK Wolf Conservation Trust}}</ref>

The Erich Klinghammer Award is given in his memory for outstanding contributions in the fields of wolf behaviour, ecology, and conservation.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ohfortheloveofscience.com/2009/11/16/carnivore-conservation-in-a-changing-world/|year=2009|title=Carnivore Conservation in the Changing World|accessdate=August 31, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111026104201/http://ohfortheloveofscience.com/2009/11/16/carnivore-conservation-in-a-changing-world/|archive-date=October 26, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>
